Outward
OWT-werd
a. & adv.
From out and the Anglo-Saxon suffix -weard, denoting direction. Webster 1828: external; exterior; visible; opposed to inward. Scripture uses the word to draw the line God draws, between what man can see and what He sees.

Biblical Definition

The verse that governs this word is the LORD’s correction of Samuel at the anointing of David: Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature... for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart (1 Samuel 16:7). Samuel was a prophet, and he had just been wrong about Eliab; the capacity to judge by appearance is not cured by office. Our Lord applies the same standard to the most religious men of His day: ye are like unto whited sepulchres, which indeed appear beautiful outward, but are within full of dead men's bones, and of all uncleanness (Matthew 23:27). The outward is not merely less important; where it is cultivated as a substitute it becomes a lie. Paul turns the word toward the believer’s body and finds comfort where the world finds only decline: though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day (2 Corinthians 4:16). And Peter directs Christian women away from the visible to the durable: Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel (1 Peter 3:3), the next verse naming the hidden man of the heart, of great price in the sight of God.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines OUTWARD as external; exterior; forming the superficial part; visible; apparent; and, in reference to the mind, foreign, adventitious, opposed to inward or spiritual.

expand to see more

OUTWARD, a. — External; exterior; forming the superficial part; as the outward form.

Visible; apparent; as outward show or profession.

Adventitious; not intrinsic; as outward circumstances.

OUTWARD, adv. — To foreign parts; as a ship outward bound.

From out and -ward, Anglo-Saxon weard, direction; the opposite of inward.

Key Scripture

1 Samuel 16:7 — "But the LORD said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart."

Matthew 23:27 — "Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye are like unto whited sepulchres, which indeed appear beautiful outward, but are within full of dead men's bones, and of all uncleanness."

2 Corinthians 4:16 — "For which cause we faint not; but though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day."

1 Peter 3:3 — "Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel;"

Modern Corruption

1 Samuel 16:7 is regularly quoted to mean that appearance does not matter at all; what it says is that God sees what man cannot, which makes the heart more accountable rather than the outward irrelevant.

expand to see more

The verse is not a licence for indifference to the visible. Scripture cares a great deal about outward conduct: it legislates it, it makes it the test of profession, and James says faith without works is dead. What 1 Samuel 16:7 denies is that the visible is sufficient evidence, and it denies this in a context where a prophet had just misjudged. The popular use of the verse — as a warrant against any assessment of a man’s life — produces the opposite of its intent, since the reason the outward cannot be trusted is that God is examining something deeper and will not be deceived. Our Lord’s woes on the Pharisees make the same point from the other side: their outward was beautiful, and that was precisely the indictment. Hypocrisy is only possible where the outward can be managed.

1 Peter 3:3-4 has been read in two wrong directions. The first is legalistic: a prohibition of braided hair, gold, and good clothing as such — which cannot be sustained, since the same grammatical construction would forbid the putting on of apparel altogether. Peter is setting a comparison, as Scripture often does, not banning the lesser thing. The second error is the modern dismissal of the passage as cultural residue. But the positive command remains and is unaffected by culture: the adorning that God prizes is the hidden man of the heart, a meek and quiet spirit, which He calls of great price. In an age organized around the curation of an outward image, that is not a quaint verse; it is a direct contradiction of the reigning economy of attention.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ayin (H5869), the eye, in the phrase to the eyes; mareh (H4758), appearance; Greek exothen (G1855), from without, outward; exo (G1854), outside.

expand to see more

Hebrew ayin (H5869) — the eye; man looketh to the eyes, rendered on the outward appearance (1 Samuel 16:7).

Hebrew lebab (H3824) — the heart, the inner man; what the LORD looks upon instead.

Greek exothen (G1855) — from the outside, outwardly; appear beautiful outward (Matthew 23:27).

Greek exo (G1854) with anthropos — the outward man; the perishing frame of 2 Corinthians 4:16.

Greek kosmos (G2889) — ordering, adornment; the root of Peter’s adorning in 1 Peter 3:3.

Usage

"Man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart (1 Samuel 16:7) — spoken to a prophet who had just misjudged."

"Appear beautiful outward, but are within full of dead men's bones (Matthew 23:27) — hypocrisy is only possible where the outward can be managed."

"Though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day (2 Corinthians 4:16) — comfort where the world sees only decline."
